title: Polynomial flip-distance bounds for three-manifold triangulations
formal:
Does every compact connected piecewise-linear three-manifold, with or without boundary, have a polynomial bound on the number of local moves needed to pass between any two of its finite simplicial triangulations?

Precisely, let \(\mathcal M_3\) be the finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulations defined below, let \(t(K)\) count tetrahedra, and write \(K\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}L\) when their realizations are piecewise-linearly homeomorphic. Prove or refute
\[
\forall R\in\mathcal M_3\ \exists C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall T,U\in\mathcal M_3:\quad
\bigl(T\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}R\ \land\ U\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}R\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\exists\text{ a legal move sequence from }T\text{ to }U
\text{ of length at most }C\bigl(t(T)+t(U)\bigr)^k.
\]
The constants may depend on the fixed reference triangulation \(R\), equivalently on its manifold type, but must work for every pair \(T,U\) of that type. No common polynomial for different manifolds, effective procedure to obtain the constants, or efficient algorithm to find a move sequence is required. Intermediate triangulations may have more tetrahedra than either endpoint.

The card uses the standard combinatorial version: finite abstract simplicial complexes, interior bistellar moves, and elementary shellings and their inverses on the boundary. This explicitly repairs the boundary convention in the original question and specifies a simplicial representation. The source also discusses more general face-pairing encodings; no unproved equivalence between their quantitative move bounds and this specified version is part of the claim.
why: Polynomial move bounds would provide short, locally checkable certificates relating arbitrary triangulations of each fixed three-manifold. A counterexample would exhibit intrinsic superpolynomial reconfiguration distance in one fixed topological space. The question measures representation changes, rather than the performance of a particular recognition algorithm.

sentences: A compact connected three-manifold can be represented by many finite simplicial triangulations.
The question asks whether each fixed manifold admits a polynomial bound, in the two endpoint tetrahedron counts, on the number of local moves connecting any pair of its triangulations.
The specified convention permits both interior bistellar flips and elementary boundary shellings and their inverses, explicitly repairing the boundary ambiguity in the original source.
Such a bound would give short certificates connecting finite descriptions of the same space without requiring an efficient method to find them or a single polynomial for every manifold.
A complete Lean answer must prove the bound for every fixed manifold type or exhibit one fixed type whose triangulation distances defeat every polynomial.

definitions:
Write \(\mathbb N_{\ge1}=\{1,2,\ldots\}\) and \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\) is a collection of subsets of a finite vertex set, containing the empty set and closed under taking subsets. Its vertex set is exactly the union of its faces. A face with \(j+1\) vertices has dimension \(j\). The complex is pure of dimension three if it is nonempty and every maximal face has four vertices. These maximal faces are its tetrahedra, and \(t(K)\) is their number. A finite encoding labels the vertices by \([n]\) and lists each four-element maximal face once, in increasing lexicographic order; every other face is its subset. There are no face self-identifications, distinct simplices with the same vertex set, geometric lengths, or ideal vertices deleted from the realization.

The realization \(|K|\) is the union of the convex hulls of the standard basis vectors indexed by each nonempty face, inside Euclidean space with one coordinate for each vertex. A simplicial isomorphism is a bijection between vertex sets that takes faces to faces in both directions. A subdivision replaces the linear simplices of a realization by finitely many linear simplices meeting along common faces, with the same union, each new simplex contained in an old one. Two complexes are piecewise-linearly homeomorphic if they admit subdivisions related by a simplicial isomorphism. This defines \(\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}\); no chosen homeomorphism or boundary marking is included as input.

For a face \(A\in K\), its link is
\[
\operatorname{lk}_K(A)=\{B\in K:B\cap A=\varnothing\text{ and }A\cup B\in K\}.
\]
The set \(\mathcal M_3\) consists of finite pure three-dimensional complexes whose realizations are connected and whose link at every vertex is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic either to the boundary of a tetrahedron or to one filled triangle. These are the two-sphere and two-ball link conditions, respectively, for a compact combinatorial three-manifold with possibly nonempty boundary. Both orientable and nonorientable manifolds are allowed. The boundary subcomplex \(\partial K\) is generated by the triangular faces lying in exactly one tetrahedron. A manifold is closed when this subcomplex has no nonempty face. Connectivity means any two vertices can be joined by a sequence of edges. Quantification over reference complexes covers precisely the compact connected PL manifold types in this convention.

Here are the permitted moves. For a finite nonempty set of vertices \(A\), let \(\Delta A\) be the simplex consisting of all its subsets, and \(\partial\Delta A\) the complex of its proper subsets. For complexes on disjoint vertex sets, their join is the complex of unions of a face from each. An interior bistellar move chooses a nonempty face \(A\in K\) and a disjoint nonempty finite vertex set \(B\), allowing new vertices, such that
\[
|A|+|B|=5,\qquad B\notin K,\qquad
\operatorname{lk}_K(A)=\partial\Delta B.
\]
It replaces \(\Delta A*\partial\Delta B\) by \(\partial\Delta A*\Delta B\), retaining their common boundary. In set notation the result is
\[
K'=\bigl(K\setminus\{\sigma\in K:A\subseteq\sigma\}\bigr)
\ \cup\ (\partial\Delta A*\Delta B).
\]
Vertices no longer contained in any nonempty face are discarded. This is one move: according to the two set sizes it replaces one tetrahedron by four, two by three, three by two, or four by one. The link and missing-face conditions rule out accidental identifications or an already present replacement simplex. Only results in \(\mathcal M_3\) are admitted.

For a boundary attachment, choose a four-element vertex set \(\sigma\) whose tetrahedron is not already in \(K\), possibly introducing new vertices. Require that
\[
D=K\cap\Delta\sigma
\]
is exactly the union, including all their subfaces, of one, two, or three distinct triangular faces of \(\sigma\), and that \(D\subseteq\partial K\). This is a triangulated two-ball in the boundary. Replace \(K\) by \(K\cup\Delta\sigma\), requiring the result to belong to \(\mathcal M_3\). The reverse of any such legal attachment is an elementary boundary shelling and is also one move. It removes the tetrahedron and precisely those of its faces absent before the attachment; it does not leave isolated unsupported lower-dimensional faces. The conditions exclude attaching a tetrahedron along no face or along its entire boundary. These boundary moves preserve the PL manifold type and allow its boundary triangulation to change.

A legal sequence is a finite sequence \(K_0,\ldots,K_\ell\in\mathcal M_3\), with \(K_0\) isomorphic to \(T\) and \(K_\ell\) isomorphic to \(U\), in which each consecutive pair is related by one of the permitted moves, allowing a simplicial relabeling. Its length is \(\ell\); relabeling itself is free, so this is a distance on isomorphism classes. A zero-length sequence is allowed for isomorphic endpoints. Every intermediate complex has the same PL manifold type, but its vertex set, tetrahedron count and boundary triangulation may vary. There is no restriction to geometric hyperbolic triangulations, fixed vertices, or size-decreasing moves.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the formal assertion or its full logical negation, for the complexes and legal moves above.

A positive answer must prove that each reference \(R\) admits some constants \(C,k\) bounding the length of a connecting sequence for every pair of triangulations of its PL type. An existence proof is sufficient; the target does not require a polynomial-time search algorithm or a uniform polynomial across all manifold types.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists R\in\mathcal M_3\ \forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists T,U\in\mathcal M_3:\quad
T\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}R\ \land\ U\simeq_{\mathrm{PL}}R\ \land\
\forall\text{ legal sequences }(K_0,\ldots,K_\ell)\text{ from }T\text{ to }U,
\quad \ell>C\bigl(t(T)+t(U)\bigr)^k.
\]
The same fixed manifold type must defeat every polynomial; choosing a different manifold as \(C,k\) vary is insufficient. A lower bound for one prescribed simplification procedure, an upper bound on only the largest intermediate triangulation, or a theorem restricted to geometric triangulations does not settle the required distance statement. Conditional complexity consequences establish only the corresponding conditional claim. The assertion is exact; numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not relax it.

context_blocks.text: Question 8 permits a different polynomial for each fixed manifold. Question 9 separately asks for independence from the manifold, and Question 10 asks about the largest intermediate triangulation. Neither additional target is included here.

The original text permits manifolds with boundary but describes only interior bistellar flips, which preserve the boundary triangulation; its stated vertex-link definition also omits ball links. This card explicitly uses the standard compact-manifold convention with sphere or ball links and elementary boundary moves.

The 2026 K3 problem list supplies the combinatorial compact-manifold setting, explicitly adding boundary shellings and distinguishing fixed-manifold from uniform move bounds. The finite simplicial model in this card follows that convention; the scope choice is editorial.

Kalelkar and Phanse give bounds for geometric triangulations of closed constant-curvature manifolds. In dimension three their bound is cubic in the two tetrahedron counts when the geometric parameters are fixed, but its coefficient depends on edge-length and injectivity-radius data absent from arbitrary combinatorial inputs.
